question: Citizens in democracies must be able to freely debate important political topics online. In this context, I call on the Commission to answer the following questions: 1.

Does the DSA, Commission guidance, or any instruments thereunder require platforms to pre-emptively moderate political speech outside of the EU simply because their content may spill over into the EU?

Does the DSA, Commission guidance, or any instruments thereunder require or encourage platforms to remove or moderate political content, such as criticism of government officials or policies, scientific debate, statistical facts, or interviews of public officials or candidates for public office?

Designated very large online platforms state that their respective content moderation policies apply globally. Does the DSA, Commission guidance, or any instruments thereunder require them to substantially modify their content moderation policies? If so, how?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.11.2026) The Digital Services Act (DSA)1, or any instruments and Commission guidance thereunder do not place any requirements on online platforms to remove or moderate access to content outside the EU, including political content.
Nothing in the DSA, or any instruments or Commission guidance thereunder requires online platforms to remove lawful content online, including any of the examples of content mentioned in the question.

Where platforms choose to impose content restrictions in their own policies in the EU, the DSA requires that such restrictions (1) are made transparent; (2) duly regard freedom of expression and information and other fundamental rights; and (3) are subject to user information and appeals processes. The Commission does not have the power, nor will it ever attempt to dictate what people can or cannot say online.

Nothing in the DSA, or any instruments and Commission guidance thereunder obliges online platforms to have global content moderation policies. The DSA applies only in the EU. Under the DSA, it is for online platforms to decide what items of lawful information are permitted on their service.

When defining their content moderation policies, online platforms are subject to the transparency, user-rights and freedom of expression safeguards, including those in relation to political content. In addition, online platforms have to assess and mitigate systemic risks in the EU stemming from the design of their systems or from how their services are used.
Valid mitigation measures can include adapting content moderation processes in the EU. All mitigation measures must always remain consistent with the fundamental rights of users.
